newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU trade ministers meet to plot WTO tactics.
newsitem.headline: EU trade ministers meet to plot WTO tactics.

text.p: European Union trade ministers begin gathering in Ireland on Wednesday to try iron out differences ahead of the World Trade Organisation ministerial meeting in Singapore in December.

Although the Dublin gathering is an informal meeting, EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan is hoping to secure tacit approval for policies to show the 15-nation bloc united on issues ranging from labour standards to relations with the U.S.
Brittan -- an unabashed champion of trade liberalisation -- is believed to have set modest targets for Singapore, but some analysts say the EU has much to be modest about.
"The rest of the world is either in no position or under no obligation to deliver much of what the EU is after," said one Asian diplomat.
"In many ways we (Asian nations) are prepared to try stop Singapore turning into a trade round instead of an examination of policies."

Diplomats from Ireland -- which holds the current EU presidency -- said the Dublin meeting aims to focus minds on steps needed to take world trade liberalisation further, but at the same time protect European industry.
"Liberalisation is a vital element for growth and prosperity in the EU," one diplomat said. "But we have to temper that with the interests of states most threatened by cheaper imports."

It is on this issue where EU officials are believed to be most divided. Brittan is under pressure -- notably from the European Parliament -- to put more pressure on developing nations for stricter adherence to European-style labour standards, including minimum wages and pension guarantees.
But Asian states in particular see this as a thinly disguised attempt to make their industries less competitive and some have have vowed to keep the issue off the agenda in Singapore.

Brittan is also to brief EU ministers on the commission's proposals for the second phase of liberalising global agreements on textiles and garments -- an area in which he feels badly let down by European trade partnmers.

Last week the European Commission -- the EU's executive -- warned that its proposals for Singapore were likely to be modest unless major textile and garment exporters swiftly came up with significant proposals of their own.

But this, say developing nations, was a cheap shot from Brittan. As part of incorporating the General Agreement on Tarrifs and Trade into the WTO, the EU is obliged by next year to open its textile markets by 17 percent of 1990's volumes.
Although major textile exporters are not obligated to similar quantitative reductions in the second phase, the Commission has said it would "back catalogue" unless there was some reciprocity.
In this way the EU could say it has met its obligations without having to offer anything new, counting instead products which have already been liberalised.
The other topic sure to provoke discussion among ministers is that of relations with the U.S. in the wake of recent laws passed in Washington which the EU considers extra-territorial.

Brittan, given a mandate by EU foreign ministers in July to examine reaction to the Helms-Burton Act and D'Amato Bill -- which seek to quash trade with Cuba and Iran and Libya respectively -- will outline the counter-proposals.
Ireland is believed to be advocating a more cautious -- or at least delayed -- response to that urged by Spain and Italy, the two countries whose business interests are most threatened.
